content: The study by Leung (2018) evaluated patients treated with combinations of ombitasvir, paritaprevir, ritonavir, ribavirin (RBV), and other direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) such as sofosbuvir (SOF) with velpatasvir (VEL), ledipasvir (LDV), or glecaprevir (GLC) with pibrentasvir (PIB). Similarly, Jonas (2019) focused on patients treated for 16 weeks, while Hirsch (2020) examined treatment durations of 12 or 24 weeks. Another study by Jonas (2021) analyzed patients treated for 8, 12, or 16 weeks. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 49 studies assessed the quality of evidence. Sustained virologic response (SVR12) was consistently reported for all patients. For young children aged 3–5 years, 41 patients were treated with SOF + VEL, 25 with GLC + PIB, and 101 with other regimens, primarily SOF + LDV. Most patients (81%) received regimens with stringent regulatory approval, and 74% were treated for 12 weeks. The majority were not infected with hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 3 (GT3). Among 167 young children across seven studies, the SVR12 rate was 95% (95% CI: 89–99%), with no evidence of heterogeneity. Efficacy was 83% for SOF + VEL, 92% for GLC + PIB, and 92–100% for other regimens. No data were available for SOF + daclatasvir (DCV). Discontinuation rates were low, with only 4% of young children discontinuing treatment due to non-virological reasons, such as difficulty taking oral medication or adverse events. For older children aged 6–11 years, 34 patients were treated with SOF + DCV, 73 with SOF + VEL, 56 with GLC + PIB, and 309 with other regimens, primarily SOF + LDV or SOF + RBV. Most patients (87%) received regimens with stringent regulatory approval, and 62% were treated for 12 weeks. The SVR12 rate among 472 older children across 13 studies was 99% (95% CI: 97–100%), with no evidence of heterogeneity. Efficacy was 100% for SOF + DCV, 93% for SOF + VEL, 96% for GLC + PIB, and 99–100% for other regimens. Discontinuation was rare, occurring in only 1% of older children. For adolescents aged 12–18 years, 183 patients were treated with SOF + DCV, 102 with SOF + VEL, 47 with GLC + PIB, and 1,896 with other regimens, primarily SOF + LDV. Most patients (87%) received regimens with stringent regulatory approval, and 85% were treated for 12 weeks. The SVR12 rate among 1,891 adolescents across 35 studies was 99% (95% CI: 98–100%), with minimal heterogeneity. Efficacy was consistent across regimens, with the lowest SVR12 rate observed in a small group treated with SOF + DCV for 24 weeks. Discontinuation was uncommon, and no virological failures were reported among adolescents with HIV-HCV coinfection. Safety data for young children showed that 72% experienced at least one adverse event, with vomiting (21%), cough (14%), and diarrhea (9%) being the most common. A serious adverse event of accidental ribavirin overdose requiring hospitalization was reported in one child, who completed treatment and achieved SVR12. For older children, 53% experienced at least one adverse event, with similar adverse event profiles.
